Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette:
Patricia, a 54-year-old chef, found herself increasingly withdrawn and on edge, a stark contrast to the vibrant, commanding presence she once held in the bustling kitchen. Her current struggles began several years ago, after a late shift when a trusted sous chef, a man she had considered a friend, assaulted her in the quiet solitude of her own restaurant. The violation shattered her sense of safety and profoundly altered her perception of the world.

Now, unexpected movements nearby, like a waiter rushing past her station or a sudden clatter of pans, cause Patricia to startle violently, her body tensing as if she is back in that moment of danger, feeling an overwhelming sense of threat. This hypervigilance means she is superalert and constantly on guard, especially in the kitchen where the proximity of male colleagues and the demands for teamwork are unavoidable. She often feels a profound sense of threat from strangers approaching her, even in ordinary situations like grocery shopping, as if anyone could harbor ill intent. This pervasive sense of threat doesn't just make her jumpy; it frequently pulls her back into fragmented memories of the assault. She experiences disjointed images and sensations, her body often feeling eerily in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, unable to articulate the full horror in words. The constant feeling of being threatened solidifies her conviction that you can never truly know who will harm you, reinforcing her deep-seated negative appraisals.

These visceral, fragmented memories, which she can't seem to put into a coherent narrative, only serve to deepen her belief that she was profoundly betrayed by someone she trusted. The raw, wordless experience of her body reliving the trauma makes it impossible for her to shake the feeling that people can't be trusted, a conviction that now colors every interaction. Consequently, these negative appraisals fuel her pervasive sense of threat; because she is certain harm can come from anywhere and anyone, she remains perpetually on guard, perceiving danger in situations others would consider benign. This ingrained mistrust makes her incredibly sensitive to certain conversation topics, especially those that touch on personal boundaries or vulnerability, and makes her perceive these as triggers.

Indeed, when Patricia finds herself in situations involving a male presence, particularly if she is alone with men, or if a conversation veers into emotionally intimate territory, these become potent triggers. These moments don't just evoke anxiety; they immediately flood her with the conviction that people can't be trusted and reignite the pain of feeling betrayed. The triggers themselves can also directly bring back the fragmented pieces of her memory, where she feels her body reenacting the frightening event, unable to form a coherent story. Her deeply held belief that people can't be trusted means she interprets more and more situations as potential triggers, making her wary of emotional closeness even with her loving husband, John, who has grown increasingly distant due to her constant emotional unavailability. This mistrust, born from betrayal, also distorts her memories of the event itself; she struggles to integrate the fragmented pieces into a whole because the overwhelming narrative in her mind is one of fundamental betrayal and the unreliability of others, rather than a linear sequence of events. The constant sense of threat she carries, the hypervigilance, further primes her to perceive male presence or certain conversation topics as dangerous, amplifying their triggering power and trapping her in a relentless cycle of fear.

Patricia finally sought help because the joy of cooking, her life's passion, has been replaced by a constant internal battle. She dreads busy shifts, avoids interacting with new male staff, and finds herself increasingly isolated, her marriage strained. What frightens her most is the tightening grip of her fear, the way it has shrunk her world, leaving her with a desperate hope that she might one day feel safe again.
